guides.title: How to fix a door that sticks or rubs
guides.description: Fix a sticking door in 30 to 60 minutes: tighten the hinges, pull a sagging door back with one long screw, and plane only if you must. Tips from DeKalb, IL.
guides.intro: Most sticking doors are not swollen. They have sagged on loose hinge screws, and you can fix that in half an hour without taking the door down.
guides.symptoms: Door scrapes the top corner, the latch side, or drags at the bottom; worse in humid summer weather.
quickCheck: Close the door slowly and watch the gap (the "reveal") around it. Even gap all around = good; a gap that pinches to nothing shows where it rubs.
Rubbing at the top latch-side corner almost always means the door has sagged on loose top hinge screws.
Rub chalk or a pencil on the door edge, close it a few times, and look for the transfer mark on the frame.

steps.title: Tighten every hinge screw
steps.detail: Tighten all hinge screws on the door and the frame. Do not plane anything until the hinges are tight — loose hinges are the most common cause.

steps.title: Pull the door back up with one long screw
steps.detail: If it still rubs at the top latch corner, replace one screw in the TOP hinge on the frame side (the one closest to the stop) with a 3-inch screw. It bites into the wall stud and pulls the jamb and door back toward the hinge side.

steps.title: Fix any stripped screw holes
steps.detail: If a screw spins without tightening, repair the hole first (see the stripped-screw-hole guide), then re-drive it.

steps.title: Check again before removing wood
steps.detail: Close the door and check the reveal. Most doors are fixed by now. If the frame or door is truly swollen, mark the tight area with a pencil.

steps.title: Plane or sand only what is needed
steps.detail: Remove the minimum: plane with long strokes toward the corners, or sand with 80-grit on a block. Take a little, test, repeat.

steps.title: Seal the bare wood
steps.detail: Prime and paint (or seal) any bare edge — top and bottom edges too if you trimmed them — so the door does not soak up moisture and swell again.

tips: Aim for a reveal of about 1/8 inch (roughly the thickness of a nickel).
A thin bead of paste wax or a candle rubbed on a lightly rubbing edge can buy time on a seasonal swell.
Plane the hinge-side edge when possible — it keeps the latch-side bevel and hardware untouched.
tools: Block plane or sanding block (80/120 grit)
parts: 3-inch hinge screws to match the finish
guides.callPro: Big cracks above the door, a frame that is clearly out of square, or doors suddenly sticking all over the house can mean the house is settling. Have it looked at before you start trimming doors.

guides.title: How to fix a door that won’t latch
guides.description: Door pops open or has to be slammed? Find where the latch misses the strike plate and fix it with a file, an adjustment or a moved strike. DeKalb, IL tips.
guides.intro: When a door won’t latch, the latch and the strike plate have drifted out of line. A little marker on the latch shows you exactly where.
guides.symptoms: You have to slam or lift the door to latch it, it pops back open, or it rattles when closed.
quickCheck: With the door open, turn the knob: does the latch move freely in and out? If not, the lockset is the problem, not the strike.
Rub lipstick, dry-erase marker or crayon on the latch tongue, close the door, and see where it marks the strike plate — above, below, or in front of the opening.
Tighten the hinges first; a sagging door is the usual reason the latch drops below the strike.

steps.title: Tighten the hinges
steps.detail: Re-tighten all hinge screws (use a 3-inch screw in the top hinge if the door has sagged). Retest — this alone fixes many doors.

steps.title: Read the mark
steps.detail: Mark low or high: the strike opening is out of line vertically. Mark toward the stop or the door won't stay shut snug: the strike needs to move closer to the stop. Door rattles: the strike tab is too far from the stop.

steps.title: Small miss (under 1/8 inch): file the opening
steps.detail: Remove the strike plate and file the edge of the opening where the latch hits. Reinstall and test.

steps.title: Adjustable strike
steps.detail: Some strikes have a small screw and sliding tab — loosen it, slide the tab toward the stop, and retighten until the door closes snug without rattling.

steps.title: Bigger miss: move the strike
steps.detail: Unscrew the plate, fill the old screw holes (glued wood plugs or toothpicks), chisel the mortise so the plate sits flush in its new spot, and drill new pilot holes. Make sure the hole behind the strike is deep enough for the latch.

steps.title: Strike set too deep
steps.detail: If the latch reaches but the door still won't hold, the strike may be recessed too deep. Shim it out with a thin piece of card or veneer behind the plate.

tips: Move a strike less than a screw-hole width? Fill the old holes first, or the new screws will wander back into them.
Weatherstripping that is too thick on an exterior door can push the door off the latch; try a thinner strip before moving hardware.
parts: Wood glue and toothpicks or a small dowel
guides.callPro: A cracked or split door frame at the strike, or a damaged strike on an exterior security door, may need the frame repaired first.

guides.title: How to fix a stripped screw hole
guides.description: A screw that spins and won’t tighten? Fill the hole with glued wood or a golf tee and re-drive it. A 20-minute fix for hinges and hardware in DeKalb, IL homes.
guides.intro: A screw that spins without tightening has chewed up its hole. A bigger screw is a short-term patch; filling the hole with glued wood is the lasting fix.
guides.symptoms: A screw turns and turns but never gets tight; a hinge or strike is loose.
quickCheck: Is the wood split or just worn? Split jambs need glue and clamping first.
Can a longer screw reach solid framing? On a door frame, often yes.

steps.title: Quick fix: longer screw
steps.detail: On a door frame, a longer screw (2½–3 inch) through the hinge into the stud behind is fast and strong. Make sure the head matches the hinge countersink.

steps.title: Wood fill: toothpicks or a dowel
steps.detail: For light loads, dip several wooden toothpicks or a whittled sliver in wood glue, pack the hole, let it dry, and trim flush. For heavy-use doors, drill the hole out (about 3/8 inch) and glue in a hardwood dowel.

steps.title: Let it dry
steps.detail: Give the glue the time on the label (typically about an hour minimum; overnight is best for a dowel).

steps.title: Pilot and re-drive
steps.detail: Drill a pilot hole in the center of the plug and drive the screw. Snug it — don't overtighten.

tips: Work one hole at a time with the other screws holding the hinge in position.
Golf tees make quick, tapered plugs for big holes.
Set the drill clutch low on the final turns — that is how most holes get stripped in the first place.
parts: Wooden toothpicks, golf tees or hardwood dowel
guides.callPro: Particleboard cabinets that crumble around the hole may need a repair kit or a new hinge location instead.

furtherReading.name: This Old House: How to repair a stripped screw hole

guides.title: How to adjust a sagging or crooked cabinet door
guides.description: Kitchen cabinet door crooked, sagging or not closing? Most hidden hinges have three adjustment screws. Fix it in minutes with a screwdriver. DeKalb, IL tips.
guides.intro: Most kitchen cabinet doors use hidden hinges with built-in adjustment screws. A few quarter-turns usually straighten a door without new parts.
guides.symptoms: Cabinet door is crooked, rubs the next door, sticks out, or won't stay closed.
quickCheck: Open it: concealed "cup" hinges inside the door are adjustable. Visible hinges on the outside have little adjustment.
Tighten the mounting screws first — many doors are fixed right there.

steps.title: Tighten mounting screws
steps.detail: Tighten the screws holding the hinge cup to the door and the mounting plate to the cabinet. If they spin, fix the stripped hole first.

steps.title: Side-to-side (front screw)
steps.detail: The screw nearest the door moves the door left or right — use it to even the gap between doors or square a crooked door.

steps.title: In-and-out (back screw)
steps.detail: The rear screw moves the door closer to or farther from the cabinet face so it sits flat when closed.

steps.title: Up-and-down (plate screws)
steps.detail: Loosen the mounting-plate screws (or turn the height cam on newer plates), slide the door up or down, and retighten.

steps.title: Adjust in small turns
steps.detail: Make quarter-turn changes, close the door, and check. On doors with 2–3 hinges, adjust each hinge the same amount so the door doesn't twist.

tips: Replacement hinges: match the overlay, cup size (35 mm is standard) and brand style; take the old one to the store.
Tall pantry doors with soft-close on every hinge can close too slowly; soft-close on some hinges is often enough.
parts: Replacement hinge matching overlay/cup size if broken
guides.callPro: Swollen or crumbling particleboard around the hinge cup needs a repair kit or a new door.

guides.title: How to fix or replace drawer slides
guides.description: Drawer sticking, sagging or falling out? Learn how to check, clean and replace ball-bearing drawer slides so drawers glide again. DeKalb, IL home tips.
guides.intro: A drawer that sticks, sags or falls out usually has a bent, loose or worn slide. Matching replacements cost little and go in with a screwdriver.
guides.symptoms: Drawer grinds, drops, comes off the track, or won't close all the way.
quickCheck: Pull the drawer out and look: metal tracks on the sides (side-mount ball-bearing), white/cream tracks with nylon wheels (epoxy roller), or nothing visible (undermount, under the drawer).
Loose screws are common — check them before buying parts.

steps.title: Remove the drawer
steps.detail: Ball-bearing: pull out fully and press the black lever on each side (one up, one down). Roller: pull out and lift the front. Undermount (e.g., Blum Tandem): squeeze the orange levers under the front and lift.

steps.title: Tighten and clean
steps.detail: Tighten all slide screws. Clean debris from the track; a light dry lubricant can help rollers.

steps.title: Measure for replacement
steps.detail: Measure the slide length (usually matching the old one), and confirm side clearance: most side-mount ball-bearing slides need 1/2 inch on each side between drawer and cabinet.

steps.title: Install the cabinet members
steps.detail: Mount the cabinet sides level and parallel, at the same height on both sides. Use the front slotted holes first so you can fine-tune.

steps.title: Install the drawer members
steps.detail: Mount the drawer members aligned with the bottom edge, set back to match the face frame. Keep each left/right pair together.

steps.title: Test and finish
steps.detail: Slide the drawer in, check the reveal around the drawer front, adjust in the slotted holes, then add the remaining screws.

tips: Bring the old slide to the store — length and mounting style must match.
Use a torpedo level and pencil marks to keep both cabinet members exactly parallel; a twist makes a new slide bind.
parts: Matching slide pair (length, mount type, load rating)
guides.callPro: Swapping side-mount slides for undermount slides usually means new drawer boxes, which is a bigger job.

furtherReading.name: Family Handyman: Fixing drawers with ball-bearing slides

guides.title: How to patch a hole in drywall
guides.description: Patch small, medium and large drywall holes so they disappear after paint: the right patch, thin coats and wide feathering. Tips from DeKalb, IL.
guides.intro: The secret to a patch that disappears is thin coats feathered wide, then primer before paint. Patience matters more than skill.
guides.symptoms: Doorknob hole, anchor holes, dents or a fist-sized hole in drywall.
quickCheck: Size decides the method: nail hole = spackle; up to about 6 inches = mesh patch; bigger = cut out and set a drywall piece on backer boards.
Before cutting, check for wires and pipes behind the wall (look in with a flashlight; avoid areas above and below outlets).

steps.title: Clean the edges
steps.detail: Cut away torn paper and loose gypsum with a utility knife so nothing bulges. Lightly sand the area.

steps.title: Small holes: spackle
steps.detail: Press lightweight spackle in with a putty knife, scrape it flush, let it dry, and add a second skim if it shrinks.

steps.title: Medium (up to ~6 inches): mesh patch
steps.detail: Stick a self-adhesive mesh or metal patch over the hole with at least 1 inch of overlap all around. Spread joint compound through and over it.

steps.title: Large: cut and back it
steps.detail: Square up the hole with a drywall saw, screw two wood backer strips inside the wall, screw in a matching drywall piece, then tape the seams.

steps.title: Feather out three thin coats
steps.detail: Each coat wider than the last — This Old House says the final coat should be about 12 inches square so the edges blend. Let each coat dry.

steps.title: Sand, prime, paint
steps.detail: Sand lightly, wipe off dust, spot-prime the patch (or it will look dull), then paint.

tips: Hold a work light flat against the wall — the raking light shows every ridge before you paint.
Setting-type compound (the powder you mix) dries hard and fast for the first coat on big patches.
A damp sponge "sands" without dust for small touch-ups.
guides.callPro: Water stains, soft or moldy drywall, or cracks that keep coming back point to a leak or settling. Find the cause before you patch.

guides.title: How to install a grab bar the right way
guides.description: Install a bathroom grab bar that holds: where to mount it, how to hit studs, drilling tile safely and testing it hard. Accessibility help in DeKalb, IL.
guides.intro: A grab bar has to hold a person’s full weight when they slip. That means mounting into studs or rated anchors, never drywall anchors or a towel bar.
guides.symptoms: Someone needs steady support at the toilet, tub or shower.
quickCheck: Think about who will use it, how they move (standing, sitting or transferring) and which hand they lead with. Mount it where they naturally reach.
Find studs or confirmed blocking. Never rely on towel-bar anchors.

steps.title: Pick height and spot
steps.detail: Horizontal bars are commonly mounted 33–36 inches above the floor (ADA reference). Adjust to the user — a vertical bar at the tub or shower entry helps with stepping in and out.

steps.title: Locate framing
steps.detail: Use a stud finder and confirm with a small test hole. Plan the bar so at least one flange (ideally both) hits a stud.

steps.title: Drill carefully
steps.detail: On tile, use a carbide or diamond tile bit, start slow without hammer mode, and use tape to keep the bit from walking. Watch for pipes behind tub walls.

steps.title: Fasten
steps.detail: Use the bar maker's screws into studs (or manufacturer-rated grab-bar anchors where no stud exists). Seal screw holes in wet areas with silicone.

steps.title: Test hard
steps.detail: Pull and push firmly in every direction. Building codes commonly call for 250 pounds of force — it should not move at all.

tips: Measure height to the top of the bar.
A diagonal bar on the tub long wall helps people who sit to bathe.
parts: Stud screws or rated grab-bar anchors
guides.callPro: Fiberglass or acrylic tub surrounds, or walls with no framing where you need the bar, may need blocking added behind the wall. That is a job for a pro.

furtherReading.name: Home Depot: How to install grab bars

guides.title: How to winterize outdoor faucets and hoses
guides.description: Protect outdoor faucets from freezing: disconnect hoses, shut and drain the spigot, and add a cover before the first hard freeze. Illinois winter tips.
guides.intro: A frozen outdoor faucet can split inside the wall and flood a basement. Twenty minutes before the first hard freeze prevents it.
quickCheck: Find each outdoor spigot and check whether it is frost-free (a long body that goes into the wall) or has a separate shutoff inside.
Look under each spigot inside the house for drips before you start.

steps.title: Disconnect hoses
steps.detail: Remove every hose — a hose left on traps water and can split even a frost-free spigot.

steps.title: Shut and drain
steps.detail: On older spigots with an inside shutoff, close it, open the outside faucet to drain, and leave it open.

steps.title: Store hoses
steps.detail: Drain and coil hoses; store them out of the sun.

steps.title: Cover
steps.detail: Add an insulated faucet cover on exposed spigots.

steps.title: Check other outdoor water
steps.detail: Empty and store rain barrels and pond pumps. Sprinkler systems need a blowout from an irrigation specialist.

tips: Leave the outside faucet open after draining so trapped water can escape.
Hang a tag on the inside shutoff: "Open in spring."
guides.callPro: A spigot that leaks inside the wall has likely frozen and cracked. That needs a licensed plumber.
